transcript:
This message comes from Kachava. A little boost goes a long way, especially when it comes to caring for your gut during the holiday season and beyond.
Introducing Kachava's new 3-in-1 digestive boost. Simply mix in to your favorite Kachava shake or any cold beverage.
Go to Kachava.com and use code NPR for 15% off your first order. That's K-A-C-H-A-V-A.com. Code NPR.
This is NPR News Now.
The latest headlines every hour.
Live from NPR News in Washington, I'm Windsor Johnston. Stocks on Wall Street opened mix this morning as investors studied a new report on wholesale inflation.
NPR's Scott Horsley reports the Dow Jones industrial average rose about 31 points in early trading.
Wholesale prices in October were up 6.5% from a year ago. That's the biggest annual increase in almost four years.
Wholesale prices rose more slowly, however, between September and October than they did the month before.
Microsoft is making progress at restoring email and other services. After a worldwide software outage that began on Thursday, the company says there's no indication the problem was the result of a deliberate attack.
And the FBI says it's recovered some of the loot from last month's giant cryptocurrency heist. $6.3 billion worth of crypto was stolen from the Binance exchange. The FBI has seized or restrained close to 20% of that total.
Scott Horsley, NPR News, Washington.
Microsoft says access to its services is improving following a worldwide outage.
Some users are still having trouble connecting and delays receiving email as the company works to clear backlogs, which they say are approaching normal levels.
Andrew Kautz is the director of security and investigations at Wired. He tells NPR the disruption stands out even among major tech outages.
It's really unprecedented in terms of its duration and scale. You know, we're looking at something like 16 hours that so many services have been down.
Last year, we saw a widespread outage on Amazon Web Services that was really disruptive. In 2024, we saw kind of a pair of outages and system crashes with Windows that impacted Microsoft and Windows users.
So, but in terms of 365, we really haven't seen anything like this and certainly not something on this scale.
Microsoft says there's no evidence so far of malicious activity behind the disruption. The prediction market, Kalshi, no longer counts the president's son among its advisers.
Donald Trump Jr. is out at the company, which lets users bet on the outcomes of real world events. NPR's Luke Garrett reports.
Prediction market, Kalshi says the company and the president's eldest son mutually agreed to part ways.
The stated reason, Donald Trump Jr. made a significant investment in Kalshi's top competitor, Polymarket.
The two prediction markets allow for users to bet billions on elections, sports and culture. During Trump's second term, both Kalshi and Polymarket have enjoyed little to no regulation from its federal regulator, the Commodity Futures Trading Commission.
CFTC staffing and enforcement have fallen dramatically, catching the attention of Capitol Hill Democrats who have vowed to investigate the agency, Kalshi and Polymarket.
Donald Trump Jr.'s departure comes as tech companies work to burnish their relationships with Democrats who will retake control of Congress in January.
Luke Garrett, NPR News, Washington.
This is NPR.
Broadway's spring season is going to be filled with Hollywood stars from Julia Roberts to Steve Carell. Jeff London reports the big ticket celebrities are also coming with big ticket costs.
Steve Carell and John C. Reilly will star in a revival of Neil Simon's The Odd Couple, and Jessica Chastain will star in a new play about an actress with dementia.
Also opening this spring is Julie Roberts with Paul Rudd in Small Mouth Sounds, a comic and touching play where hardly anyone speaks.
These productions will be open for limited runs, and given the limited supply of seats available, ticket prices are high.
If you want to see Julia Roberts from the best seats, be prepared to fork out almost $650.
For NPR News, I'm Jeff London in New York.
A Democratic political group is launching an effort to address voters' concerns about artificial intelligence ahead of the 2028 presidential election.
The organization is planning to spend more than a million dollars studying public views on AI and how Democrats should talk about it.
The announcement coincides with a gathering of party leaders in Denver to celebrate their midterm wins and plan what comes next.
President Trump is pushing for rapid AI development, while some Democrats are calling for tighter rules or to slow down development.
Stocks are trading lower at this hour on Wall Street.
The Dow was down 19 points, the NASDAQ down 249.
This is NPR News in Washington.
At NPR, there's a little something for everyone. If you need advice for that big life change, try listening to LifeKit.
If you want to know more about that new TV show, check out Pop Culture Happy Hour.
And if you want to dive deeper into your favorite podcasts and enjoy perks like bonus episodes, archive access and more, check out NPR Plus.
Find out more and support the shows you love at plus.npr.org.

topics.text: Wholesale inflation rose 6.5% from a year ago in October, the biggest annual jump in nearly four years
Microsoft restores email and services after a worldwide 16-hour outage with no sign of attack
FBI says it has recovered close to 20% of the $6.3 billion stolen in the Binance crypto heist
Donald Trump Jr. departs prediction market Kalshi after investing in competitor Polymarket
Broadway spring season features Hollywood stars Julia Roberts, Steve Carell, and Jessica Chastain with high ticket prices
Democratic political group launches over $1 million effort to study voter views on artificial intelligence before 2028
